headline: spot at the top of its three-year range, up 77% in a year — with next winter, not the whole horizon, the expensive part of the curve
commentary: UK power spot has printed £129.37/MWh — the top of its three-year range and up 77% on the £73 of a year ago. On a three-year view the direction is unambiguous: the market spent most of 2024 between £56 and £75, climbed through 2025, and has accelerated since the spring, so anything contracted now is being priced against the highest baseline since the 2022 crisis unwound. Gas is doing the driving: NBP front-month is 161.85 p/therm and the winter curve has kept inflating — Dec 26 at 169.08, Jan 27 at 169.80, Winter 26 at 164.80. Ofgem's 4% domestic price-cap rise for October, announced this week and attributed almost entirely to wholesale gas, is the same pressure surfacing in household bills. The half-hourly day-ahead market shows how uneven the day has become: across 22-28 August the evening peak cleared £136-156/MWh while midday troughs fell to £65-92. What matters most for tender timing is the shape of the forward curve. Summer 27 is priced at 107 p/therm and Winter 27 at 104, against Winter 26 at 164.80 — and both have held at or above those levels for the past fortnight, so this is a settled view of the curve rather than a one-day quirk. The expensive period is next winter, not the years beyond it. A 12-month term starting this October sits squarely on that winter; a 24-month term blends it with a materially cheaper 2027/28, which is why the longer terms are currently pricing better per kWh than the 12-month. The read: at these levels the question is term length, not whether to wait for a lower entry.

gas.note: NBP front-month (Sep 26) is 161.85 p/therm, up 0.5% on the day. The winter curve has kept inflating — Dec 26 at 169.08, Jan 27 at 169.80, Winter 26 at 164.80 — while Summer 27 (107.00) and Winter 27 (104.00) sit far lower and have held there for the past fortnight.
